entries.title: Meringues: French, Swiss and Italian
entries.summary: Egg white whipped with sugar into a glossy foam, made three ways: French with raw whites, Swiss warmed over a bain-marie, a bowl set over simmering water, and Italian with hot syrup. Each has its strengths and faults, and all three need a clean bowl.
entries.guest: Meringue is egg white whipped with sugar until glossy. On our Lemon Tart it is piped and toasted, soft and marshmallowy, against the sharp yuzu mousse and lemon jelly.

paras: A meringue is egg white whipped with sugar into a glossy foam that holds its shape. Whipping unfolds the proteins in the white, and they knit into a thin film around each air bubble; the sugar dissolves into that film and makes it thicker, glossier and slower to collapse. Baked low and long, a meringue dries crisp; toasted, it browns like a marshmallow; folded in, it lightens a mousse or a soufflé.

There are three methods, and they differ in how much heat the whites meet. French uses raw whites and is the lightest and least stable. Swiss warms the whites and sugar together before whipping. Italian cooks the whites with hot syrup and is the most stable.

French: whip the whites in a spotless bowl to soft peaks, then add the sugar a spoonful at a time, whipping well between each, until stiff, glossy and no longer gritty between the fingers. Sugar added too early slows the foam; added all at once, it knocks it flat. Dry it in a cool oven, about 90 to 100°C (194 to 212°F), for one and a half to two hours.

Swiss: whisk the whites and sugar in a bowl over simmering water until the sugar dissolves and the mix reaches 60 to 70°C (140 to 158°F), then whip off the heat until thick, glossy and cool. It is denser and silkier than French and pipes cleanly.

Italian: boil sugar with about a third of its weight in water to 118 to 121°C (244 to 250°F), firm ball to the very start of hard ball, while the whites whip to soft peaks. Pour the syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl, mixer running, never onto the whisk, and whip until barely warm. The syrup partly cooks the whites, so the foam holds for hours, needs no baking and stands up to butter in buttercream.

Most meringues use about twice the weight of sugar to white: 200 g (7 oz) of sugar to 100 g (3.5 oz) of white, roughly three large whites. That bakes crisp and holds; a soft topping can drop towards equal weights. Cream of tartar, a fine acid powder left over from winemaking, about 1 g for each 100 g of white, steadies a French meringue.

Read the peaks by lifting the whisk. Soft peaks slump over at once; firm peaks hold, the tip curling like a wave; stiff peaks stand straight up. Soft peaks suit folding, stiff peaks piping and baking.

French meringue makes crisp shells, the poached spoonfuls of œufs à la neige (snow eggs, floated on crème anglaise and now often called île flottante), the vacherin (a ring of crisp meringue filled with cream or ice cream) and, folded in, soufflés. A pavlova adds cornflour and vinegar for a crisp shell over a soft centre. The cooked meringues, Italian above all, make toasted tops for tarts, baked Alaska, where the foam shields cold ice cream from a hot oven, and buttercream.

Fat is the enemy. A trace of yolk, a greasy bowl or a plastic bowl holding old fat stops the whites foaming, because fat gets between the proteins and keeps them from forming their film. Separate each egg over a small bowl, so one broken yolk spoils one white, and wipe the bowl and whisk with lemon juice first.

Whites whipped past stiff turn dry and lumpy and will weep: a fresh white whisked in saves them for folding, but not for piping. Beads of syrup on a baked meringue mean undissolved sugar or too hot an oven. A topping that pools liquid underneath was not cooked through below.

On the Lemon Tart the meringue is piped and toasted, so its peaks caramelise into a crisp shell over a soft, marshmallow centre, sweet against the yuzu mousse, lemon jelly and sweet pastry crumb. Italian and Swiss meringues, being cooked, hold their shape on a plate and can be browned with a torch; which of the two the pastry kitchen makes, and how it browns it, is a question for the chef.

Keep it plain at the table: egg white whipped with sugar, piped and toasted. The Lemon Tart is the lightest dessert, the one to offer after a rich meal. Any egg or allergy question goes to the kitchen and the service note, never an answer from memory.

faults.fault: The whites will not foam beyond a loose froth
faults.cause: A trace of yolk or fat in the whites, the bowl or the whisk.
faults.fix: Start again in a clean bowl wiped with lemon juice, separating each egg over a small bowl first.

faults.cause: Whipped past stiff peaks, so the protein film tore.
faults.fix: For folding, whisk in one fresh white for a few seconds to loosen it; for piping or baking, start again and stop at stiff, glossy peaks.

faults.fault: Beads of sugary syrup on a baked meringue
faults.cause: Sugar not fully dissolved, or an oven that ran too hot.
faults.fix: Add the sugar slowly until no grit remains, and dry the meringue low and slow.

faults.fault: Hard threads of sugar in an Italian meringue
faults.cause: The syrup was poured onto the spinning whisk.
faults.fix: Pour in a thin stream down the side of the bowl, between whisk and wall.

faults.fault: A pool of liquid under a meringue topping
faults.cause: The meringue was not cooked through underneath.
faults.fix: Use a cooked meringue, or spread it over a hot filling and seal it to the crust.

cards.front: What are the three ways to make a meringue?
cards.back: French, raw whites with sugar added gradually; Swiss, whites and sugar warmed over a bain-marie, a bowl over simmering water, then whipped; Italian, hot syrup poured into whipping whites.

cards.front: Why is French meringue the lightest and least stable?
cards.back: Its whites are never heated, so the foam rests on raw protein alone; it must be baked dry or folded in at once.

cards.front: How warm do the whites and sugar get for a Swiss meringue?
cards.back: About 60 to 70°C (140 to 158°F) over simmering water, until the sugar dissolves, then whipped off the heat until thick and cool.

cards.front: To what temperature is the syrup cooked for an Italian meringue?
cards.back: 118 to 121°C (244 to 250°F), firm ball to the very start of hard ball, then poured in a thin stream into the whipping whites.

cards.front: Where does the hot syrup go as it is poured into the whites?
cards.back: Down the side of the bowl in a thin stream, never onto the whisk, which flings it into hard threads.

cards.front: Which meringue is the most stable, and why?
cards.back: Italian: the hot syrup partly cooks the whites, so it holds for hours, can be served unbaked and stands up to butter in buttercream.

cards.front: How do soft, firm and stiff peaks differ?
cards.back: Soft peaks slump over at once; firm peaks hold with the tip curling like a wave; stiff peaks stand straight up, glossy.

cards.front: Why does a trace of yolk or grease ruin a meringue?
cards.back: Fat gets between the white's proteins and stops them forming the film that holds each air bubble, so the foam never rises.

cards.front: What is the usual ratio of sugar to egg white for a crisp meringue?
cards.back: About two to one by weight: 200 g (7 oz) of sugar to 100 g (3.5 oz) of white, roughly three large whites.

cards.front: Why do beads of syrup form on a baked meringue?
cards.back: The sugar was not fully dissolved or the oven ran too hot; add the sugar slowly and dry meringues low and slow.

cards.front: Name three uses for a cooked meringue.
cards.back: Toasted tops on tarts, baked Alaska, where the foam shields the ice cream from the oven, and meringue buttercream.

cards.front: How is the meringue on Brennan's Lemon Tart finished?
cards.back: Piped and toasted so the peaks brown like marshmallow, beside yuzu mousse, lemon jelly and sweet pastry crumb; which meringue the kitchen makes is a question for the chef.

questions.q: Which meringue is made by pouring hot sugar syrup into whipping egg whites?
questions.why: Italian meringue whips hot syrup into the whites; Swiss warms the whites and sugar together first, and French uses raw whites with the sugar added gradually.

questions.q: To about what temperature are the whites and sugar warmed for a Swiss meringue?
questions.why: Warm enough to dissolve the sugar and begin to cook the whites, but well short of scrambling them; the hotter figure is the Italian syrup.

questions.q: What temperature does the syrup reach for an Italian meringue?
questions.why: Firm ball to the edge of hard ball: hot enough to cook the whites as it streams in, short of the hard crack and amber caramel stages.

questions.q: Which of the three meringues is the most stable?
questions.answer: Italian: hot syrup partly cooks it
distractors: French: raw whites give the firmest foam
Swiss: whipped cold, it never collapses
Any of them, once whipped past stiff
questions.why: The hot syrup sets the protein film as it whips, so Italian meringue holds for hours and stands up to butter; French, on raw whites, is the least stable.

questions.q: A batch of whites will not whip beyond a loose froth. What is the likeliest cause?
questions.answer: A trace of yolk or fat in the bowl
distractors: The whites were at room temperature
The sugar went in a spoonful at a time
A pinch of cream of tartar
questions.why: Fat keeps the proteins from forming their film around the air; room-temperature whites, slow sugar and cream of tartar all help a meringue.

questions.q: How does a stiff peak look when you lift the whisk?
questions.answer: It stands straight up and holds
distractors: It curls over like a wave
It falls from the whisk in a ribbon
questions.why: Soft peaks slump and firm peaks curl at the tip; a stiff peak stands upright, the stage for piping and baking.

questions.q: Where should the hot syrup go as it is poured into whipping whites?
questions.answer: Down the side of the bowl
distractors: All at once into the centre
Into the bowl before the whites
questions.why: Syrup that hits the whisk is flung against the bowl and sets in hard threads; a thin stream down the side folds in smoothly.

questions.q: How is the meringue on Brennan's Lemon Tart finished?
questions.answer: Piped and toasted until the peaks brown
questions.why: The toasted meringue is piped and browned so the peaks caramelise like marshmallow, sweet and soft against the yuzu mousse and lemon jelly.

entries.title: Caramel and the sugar stages
entries.summary: Sugar boiled through its named stages, from thread to hard crack and into caramel, read by thermometer and by colour. It can be made dry or wet, is stopped with warm cream and runs through Brennan's desserts, from the Foster to the bread pudding.
entries.guest: Caramel is sugar cooked until it turns amber and nutty. On our bread pudding it becomes a whiskey caramel, and in The Snickers a silky caramel custard.

paras: As a sugar syrup boils, water leaves it and the temperature climbs; the hotter it gets, the less water is left and the harder the sugar sets as it cools. Pastry cooks name those points as stages. Once almost all the water has gone, from about 160°C (320°F), the sugar itself begins to break down and brown: that is caramel, and with the colour come new flavours, nutty and toasty, then bitter. Each stage is a tool: thread for syrups and glazes, soft ball for fudge and pralines, firm ball for Italian meringue, hard ball for nougat and marshmallow, soft crack for butterscotch, hard crack for spun sugar, caramel for sauces and custards.

Read the stages with a sugar thermometer, or drop a little syrup into cold water. Thread, 106 to 112°C (223 to 234°F), falls in a fine thread. Soft ball, 112 to 116°C (234 to 241°F), makes a ball that flattens in the hand. Firm ball, 118 to 120°C (244 to 248°F), holds but gives. Hard ball, 121 to 130°C (250 to 266°F), holds firm. Soft crack, 132 to 143°C (270 to 289°F), sets hard but bends. Hard crack, 149 to 154°C (300 to 309°F), snaps clean. Authors draw the lines a degree or two apart, so follow the recipe in hand.

A wet caramel starts with sugar and about a third of its weight in water, stirred over medium heat until dissolved. Once it boils, stop stirring: swirl the pan, and wash crystals from the sides with a wet pastry brush. A spoonful of glucose or a few drops of lemon juice guards against crystallising, because they get in the way of the sugar re-forming into grains. A dry caramel is sugar alone, spread in a heavy pan and melted from the edges inward, swirled as it liquefies: quicker, deeper in flavour and easier to scorch.

Past 160°C (320°F), read the colour: pale straw, golden, then amber at about 170 to 180°C (338 to 356°F), then mahogany. Amber suits most sauces and custards. Past deep amber the sugar turns bitter within seconds, and the hot pan carries it on after it leaves the flame, so take it off a shade early.

To stop a caramel, take it off the heat and add warm cream or butter in stages, or dip the base of the pan in cold water. Cream boils up hard and throws scalding steam, so stand back, keep your face and arms clear and use a long whisk. Caramel is far hotter than boiling water and clings to skin: never taste it from the spoon, cool any burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, never ice, and tell the chef.

A caramel sauce is amber caramel loosened with cream and a little butter and salt, about equal weights of sugar and cream. Crème caramel is a custard baked in a mould lined with caramel, which melts into a thin sauce as it rests and floods the plate when the custard is turned out. Praline is nuts set in caramel, then crushed or ground; nougatine is caramel with flaked almonds, rolled thin while warm and cut or shaped.

A syrup that clouds and turns sandy was stirred after it boiled, or seeded by a crystal on the side of the pan: add water, dissolve it and begin again. A dry caramel that burns in patches was heated too fast or not swirled. Caramel that seizes into lumps met cold cream: stir it over low heat until smooth. Black, bitter caramel cannot be saved.

Caramel runs through the dessert menu. Bananas Foster begins with butter, brown sugar and cinnamon bubbled to a blond caramel, kept light so it does not set into toffee on the cold ice cream. The New Orleans Bread Pudding carries a whiskey caramel, amber caramel loosened with cream and butter, the whiskey bringing vanilla and oak. The Snickers has a caramel custard, kin to crème caramel. On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, charring drives water from the pineapple and caramelises its sugars. Which whiskey goes into the caramel is a question for the chef, and guests who avoid alcohol are told it carries whiskey.

faults.cause: Stirred after it boiled, or seeded by a sugar crystal on the side of the pan.
faults.fix: Add water, dissolve it again and restart; swirl rather than stir, and brush the sides with water.

faults.cause: Heated too fast, or not swirled as it melted.
faults.fix: Use a heavy pan over medium heat and swirl as the edges liquefy.

faults.fault: Lumps when the cream goes in
faults.cause: Cold cream set the hot caramel.
faults.fix: Stir over low heat until the lumps melt; warm the cream next time.

faults.cause: Taken past deep amber, or left in a hot pan after the heat was off.
faults.fix: It cannot be saved: start again and take it off the heat a shade early.

components: Bananas, butter, brown sugar and cinnamon
brennans.how: Butter and brown sugar are bubbled with cinnamon to a blond caramel, kept light because a darker caramel would harden into toffee on the cold vanilla ice cream.
Sugar cooked to amber, loosened with cream and butter, with whiskey for vanilla, oak and warmth; it holds in service better than a classic whiskey sauce bound with egg.
Eggs and cream cooked gently with sugar taken to amber, the silky caramel layer of the candy bar, from the same family as crème caramel and flan.
The upside-down tart of fruit caramelised in butter and sugar; pineapple is wetter than apple, so charring drives off water and caramelises its sugars while keeping its tang.

cards.front: Name the sugar stages in order, from the coolest.
cards.back: Thread, soft ball, firm ball, hard ball, soft crack, hard crack, then caramel: each hotter, with less water and a harder set.

cards.front: What is the soft ball stage, and what is it for?
cards.back: 112 to 116°C (234 to 241°F): a drop in cold water forms a soft ball that flattens; the stage for fudge and New Orleans pralines.

cards.front: How does syrup at the firm ball stage behave in cold water, and what is it for?
cards.back: At 118 to 120°C (244 to 248°F) a drop forms a ball that holds its shape but gives when pressed: the stage for chewy caramels and for the syrup of an Italian meringue.

cards.front: How does syrup at hard crack behave in cold water?
cards.back: It sets brittle and snaps clean, at 149 to 154°C (300 to 309°F): the stage for spun sugar and glassy decorations.

cards.front: At what temperature does sugar begin to become caramel?
cards.back: From about 160°C (320°F), once almost all the water has gone and the sugar itself begins to break down and brown.

cards.front: What is the difference between a dry and a wet caramel?
cards.back: Dry is sugar alone, melted in an even layer: quick, deeper and easy to scorch. Wet starts with water: slower and easier to control.

cards.front: How do you keep a wet caramel from crystallising?
cards.back: Dissolve the sugar before it boils, then swirl rather than stir; brush the sides with water, and add a little glucose or lemon juice.

cards.front: What colours does caramel pass through, and where does it turn bitter?
cards.back: Pale straw, golden, amber, then mahogany; past deep amber it turns bitter in seconds, so take it off the heat a shade early.

cards.front: How do you stop a caramel and turn it into a sauce?
cards.back: Off the heat, add warm cream or butter in stages, standing back: the cream boils up hard and throws scalding steam.

cards.front: Why is a sugar burn so severe?
cards.back: Caramel is far hotter than boiling water and clings to skin; never taste from the spoon, and cool any burn under cool running water for 20 minutes.

cards.front: How does crème caramel make its own sauce?
cards.back: The custard bakes over a layer of caramel in the mould; as it rests the caramel melts into a thin sauce that floods the plate when it is turned out.

cards.front: Name four places caramel shows on Brennan's dessert menu.
cards.back: The blond pan caramel of the Bananas Foster, the whiskey caramel on the bread pudding, the caramel custard in The Snickers and the charred pineapple of the Tarte Tatin.

questions.q: Which sugar stage comes straight after soft ball as the syrup grows hotter?
questions.why: The order runs thread, soft ball, firm ball, hard ball, soft crack, hard crack, then caramel, with less water left at each.

questions.q: A drop of syrup in cold water forms a soft ball that flattens when you lift it out. Which stage has it reached?
questions.why: Soft ball holds together in cold water but flattens in the fingers; thread only trails, firm ball holds its shape but gives, and hard crack snaps clean.

questions.q: From about what temperature does sugar begin to turn into caramel?
questions.why: Only once almost all the water has gone does the sugar itself break down and brown; boiling point and firm ball come far earlier.

questions.q: What helps keep a wet caramel from crystallising?
distractors: Stirring hard all the way through
Adding cold cream as it boils
questions.why: Glucose or acid gets in the way of the sugar re-forming into grains, and stirring or stray crystals seed the whole pan.

questions.q: At what point does a caramel cross from rich to bitter?
distractors: As soon as the sugar melts
questions.why: Straw, golden and amber build flavour; past deep amber the sugar burns within seconds, and the hot pan carries it on.

questions.q: Why is cream added to hot caramel off the heat, in stages, standing back?
questions.answer: It boils up and throws scalding steam
distractors: It makes the sugar crystallise at once
questions.why: Caramel is far hotter than boiling water, so the cream's water flashes to steam and the pan boils up hard; burns from it are severe.

questions.q: What do cooks mean by a dry caramel?
questions.answer: Sugar melted alone, with no water
distractors: Caramel left to cool and set
questions.why: A dry caramel melts sugar straight in the pan, quicker and deeper in flavour; a wet caramel dissolves it in water first.

questions.q: On which Brennan's dessert does caramel come as a silky caramel custard?
questions.why: The Snickers' caramel custard, kin to crème caramel, plays the candy bar's caramel layer; the bread pudding takes a whiskey caramel and the Tatin a charred, caramelised pineapple.

entries.title: Bananas Foster
entries.summary: Bananas turned in a caramel of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, loosened with banana liqueur, flamed with dark rum and spooned warm over vanilla ice cream. The fruit must be ripe but firm and the caramel smooth and blond before the rum is lit.
entries.guest: Bananas Foster is bananas cooked in a caramel of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, flamed with rum and spooned warm over our housemade vanilla ice cream.

paras: Bananas Foster is a pan dessert built in minutes: butter, brown sugar and cinnamon melted into a bubbling caramel, banana liqueur to loosen it, bananas turned until just soft, then dark rum added and set alight. Fruit and sauce, glossy and buttery, are spooned warm over cold vanilla ice cream, so hot meets cold in every spoonful. Each step has a reason, and a cook who knows them makes it the same way every time, in the kitchen or at the guéridon (gay-ree-DOHN), the tableside cart.

The proportions are simple: one banana a person, about three times as much brown sugar as butter by weight, a pinch of cinnamon, and banana liqueur and rum in equal measure. At Brennan's, follow the house procedure you are trained on rather than any recipe found elsewhere, and never quote quantities to a guest.

Melt the butter in a wide pan over medium heat, add the brown sugar and cinnamon, and stir until the sugar has dissolved and the mixture bubbles into a smooth, blond caramel, the butter held in the sauce rather than floating on it. Stir in the banana liqueur. Cut each banana in half lengthwise, then across, so the pieces lie flat.

Lay the bananas in the caramel and cook until they begin to soften, a minute or two, then turn them once and spoon the sauce over. Take the pan off the flame, add the measured rum, return it and tilt the far edge towards the flame to light it, away from you and the guests; the flame technique and its rules have their own entries. Baste as the flame burns out and the caramel deepens. Lay the bananas over the ice cream, then pour the warm sauce over them.

Choose bananas ripe but firm: fully yellow, sweet and fragrant, with few or no brown spots. Underripe fruit tastes starchy and stays hard; a soft, speckled banana is sweeter but collapses into purée in the hot caramel. The pan only warms the fruit and softens its outside, so the banana must arrive sweet and firm.

Get the caramel smooth before the fruit goes in. The cool bananas and their juice drop the heat, so undissolved sugar stays as grit, and a split caramel, butter pooling on top, will not come back together around the fruit. If it splits, take it off the heat and whisk in a spoonful of liqueur or water until glossy.

The rum must be warm enough to light. What burns is alcohol vapour, not the liquid, and cold rum in a pan that has cooled gives off too little to catch; a hot pan warms it in seconds. A flame that will not take is never chased with more spirit from the bottle.

The Foster belongs to the flamed fruit desserts. Cherries jubilee, generally credited to Escoffier, is cherries in syrup lit with spirit. The house guide also prints a Cherries Jubilee, tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce flamed over the same housemade vanilla ice cream, but it is not on the current dessert menu: confirm with a manager before offering it. Crêpes Suzette are thin pancakes warmed in an orange butter sauce and flamed with orange liqueur. Behind them stand the caramelised bananas of home kitchens, fried in butter and brown sugar, where the Foster began.

World Famous Bananas Foster is on the menu at every meal, made at the table for two or more. The house keeps the caramel blond and bubbling and turns ripe but firm bananas, halved and quartered, just once. The menu prints rum; the house's published recipe adds banana liqueur, which loosens the caramel and deepens the banana flavour, while dark rum brings molasses, spice and the strength to catch. Which rum the kitchen pours is a question for the chef. The vanilla ice cream is made in house.

The story and the cart belong to Bananas Foster at the table. Flaming burns the vapour above the pan, not all the alcohol in it, so much of the rum and liqueur stays in the sauce: tell any guest who avoids alcohol, and steer them to the Lemon Tart or the Pineapple Tarte Tatin. Send every question about what is in the ice cream to the kitchen.

faults.cause: Fruit too ripe, or left too long in the caramel.
faults.fix: Choose ripe but firm bananas and turn them once, just until they soften.

faults.cause: The sugar had not dissolved, or the caramel split, before the cool fruit went in.
faults.fix: Stir until smooth and blond first; whisk a split caramel off the heat with a spoonful of liqueur or water.

faults.cause: The rum or the pan was too cool to give off enough vapour.
faults.fix: Let the pan heat the rum for a few seconds; never add more spirit from the bottle.

faults.fault: The sauce sets hard on the ice cream
faults.cause: The caramel was taken past blond towards toffee.
faults.fix: Keep the caramel blond and bubbling, and loosen it with the liqueur.

brennans.how: Butter, brown sugar and cinnamon bubbled to a blond caramel, ripe but firm bananas turned once, then rum lit at the table and all spooned over the house's own vanilla ice cream. The published recipe adds banana liqueur; confirm the cart build and the rum with the kitchen.

cards.front: What is the order of the Bananas Foster build?
cards.back: Butter, brown sugar and cinnamon to a smooth caramel; banana liqueur; the bananas, turned once; then dark rum, added off the flame and lit.

cards.front: Which bananas make a good Bananas Foster, and why?
cards.back: Ripe but firm: sweet and fully yellow, yet firm enough to lift whole, so they soften in the caramel without collapsing into purée.

cards.front: How are the bananas cut for the pan?
cards.back: Halved lengthwise, then across, so each piece lies flat in the caramel and softens evenly; they are turned only once.

cards.front: Why must the caramel be smooth before the bananas go in?
cards.back: The cool fruit and its juice drop the heat, so undissolved sugar stays gritty and a split, greasy caramel will not come back around the fruit.

cards.front: Why must the rum be warm enough to light?
cards.back: It is the vapour that burns, not the liquid; a hot pan warms the rum in seconds so it gives off enough vapour to catch.

cards.front: Why is the Foster's caramel kept blond rather than dark?
cards.back: A darker caramel hardens into toffee when it meets the cold ice cream; blond and bubbling, it stays a glossy, pourable sauce.

cards.front: What does banana liqueur do in the pan?
cards.back: It loosens the caramel and deepens the banana flavour before the rum is lit; the house's published recipe uses it beside the rum.

cards.front: Does flaming burn off all the alcohol in Bananas Foster?
cards.back: No. The flame burns the vapour above the pan; much of the rum and liqueur stays in the sauce, so tell guests who avoid alcohol and steer them to the Lemon Tart or the Pineapple Tarte Tatin.

cards.front: How do the banana liqueur and the rum compare, and whose quantities rule at Brennan's?
cards.back: Equal measures of each. At Brennan's the build is the house procedure you are trained on, and the quantities are never quoted to a guest.

cards.front: Name two flamed desserts in the same family as Bananas Foster.
cards.back: Cherries jubilee, cherries in syrup lit with spirit, and crêpes Suzette, thin pancakes in an orange butter sauce flamed with orange liqueur.

cards.front: What does Bananas Foster sit on at Brennan's?
cards.back: Housemade vanilla ice cream: the bananas go over it, then the warm sauce, so hot meets cold. What goes into the ice cream is a question for the kitchen.

questions.q: In the Bananas Foster build, what goes into the pan once the caramel is smooth and before the bananas?
distractors: A splash of cream to loosen it
questions.why: The liqueur loosens the caramel and deepens the banana flavour; the bananas follow, and the rum goes in last, off the flame.

questions.q: Which bananas suit a Bananas Foster best?
distractors: Frozen, then thawed in the pan
questions.why: Ripe fruit is sweet, and firm fruit softens in the hot caramel without collapsing; speckled bananas turn to purée.

questions.q: Why is the caramel made smooth before the bananas go in?
questions.answer: The cool fruit drops the heat, leaving grit
distractors: The bananas need a crust of sugar crystals
The rum dissolves any grains later
A smooth caramel burns less in the flame
questions.why: Once the fruit and its juice cool the pan, undissolved sugar stays gritty and a split caramel will not come back together.

questions.q: The rum will not catch. What is the likeliest reason?
questions.answer: The rum and the pan were too cool
distractors: Too much butter in the caramel
The cinnamon went in too late
questions.why: Alcohol vapour burns, not the liquid; cold rum in a cooled pan gives off too little, and it is never chased with more spirit.

questions.q: Why does the house keep the Foster's caramel blond and bubbling?
questions.answer: Darker, it sets to toffee on ice cream
distractors: A blond caramel lights more easily
A dark caramel splits the liqueur
The cinnamon burns in a dark caramel
questions.why: Taken darker, the sugar sets hard as it meets the cold ice cream; blond, it stays a glossy, pourable sauce.

questions.q: A guest who avoids alcohol asks whether the flame burns it all off. What is true?
questions.answer: Much of the alcohol stays in the sauce
distractors: Only the liqueur remains, not the rum
The alcohol turns to sugar in the caramel
questions.why: The flame burns the vapour above the pan, not all the alcohol in it, so the guest is told and steered to another dessert.

questions.q: Which dessert belongs to the same flamed family as Bananas Foster?
questions.why: Crêpes Suzette are flamed with orange liqueur in the pan, like the Foster and cherries jubilee; a brûlée is torched sugar, not flamed spirit.

questions.q: What do the bananas and sauce go over at Brennan's?
questions.why: The house makes its own vanilla ice cream as the cold stage for the hot Foster; any question about what is in it goes to the kitchen.

entries.title: New Orleans bread pudding
entries.say: As it reads: New Orleans bread pudding.
entries.summary: Stale French bread soaked in a sweet, spiced custard and baked until just set, served warm with a whiskey sauce. A thrift dish New Orleans made its own, because the city's light bread drinks custard without turning to paste.
entries.guest: Our bread pudding is served warm with a whiskey caramel, tangy buttermilk ice cream and pralines, the New Orleans pecan candy, for crunch.

paras: Bread pudding is stale bread given a second life. The bread is torn or cubed, soaked in a custard of milk or cream, eggs, sugar, vanilla and spice, often with raisins, then baked until the custard sets around it. The top crisps and browns; inside it is soft, sweet and custardy, closer to a baked custard than to bread. It began as a European way to use up bread, and in New Orleans it became a staple, served warm with a sauce, usually whiskey.

Recipes vary, so follow the house recipe in hand. A sound starting point is about 450 g (1 lb) of day-old French bread to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of milk, or milk and cream, with 4 to 6 eggs, 150 to 250 g (5 to 9 oz) of sugar, vanilla, cinnamon, nutmeg and a handful of raisins. More cream makes it richer and softer; more egg makes it firmer. The test is the soak: the bread saturated, but not swimming.

Tear or cube the bread, crust and all, into a buttered dish, with the raisins scattered through. Whisk the eggs and sugar, then the milk, vanilla and spice, and pour the custard over. Press the bread down so it drinks, and rest it for 20 to 30 minutes, or covered overnight in the fridge, pressing once or twice. The rest lets the custard reach the centre of every piece, so no dry cores bake through.
Bake at about 175°C (347°F) for 45 minutes to an hour, until puffed, golden and set. A water bath, the dish set in a tray of hot water, gives gentler heat and a smoother custard.

New Orleans French bread suits it because of its crumb: light, airy and thin crusted, with little fat or sugar of its own. It stales within a day, and stale bread has dried enough to soak up a great deal of custard while keeping its shape. A dense or rich loaf drinks slowly and bakes heavy; fresh bread turns to paste.

It is done when it is set at the centre: a knife pushed in near the middle comes out clean, and only the very middle wobbles when the dish is nudged. A probe there reads about 71 to 77°C (160 to 171°F). Underbaked, it is wet and eggy inside. Baked too long or too hot, the custard curdles, weeping liquid and turning grainy and dry. A pool of custard under the bread means too much liquid or too short a soak.

Whiskey sauce is the classic partner: butter and sugar melted together, bound with a beaten egg or with cream, finished with bourbon and poured warm. A typical proportion is 115 g (4 oz) of butter, 200 g (7 oz) of sugar, one egg and 30 to 60 ml (2 to 4 tbsp) of bourbon. Whisk a little of the hot butter and sugar into the egg, return it and whisk off the heat until it thickens, then add the bourbon. Too hot, and the egg scrambles and the sauce splits; a sauce bound with cream holds better.

Bread pudding has been in New Orleans cookbooks since the nineteenth century, and the Picayune's Creole Cook Book, in its 1901 edition, already prints one. The city's French bread stales fast, and nothing went to waste. The warm whiskey sauce came later: restaurants revived the dessert from the 1970s with whiskey and bourbon sauces, and it is now the signature.

At Brennan's the New Orleans Bread Pudding comes with a whiskey caramel rather than the classic sauce: amber caramel loosened with cream and butter, with whiskey for vanilla and oak, steadier in service than a sauce bound with egg. Buttermilk ice cream brings a gentle tang that cools the warm pudding and cuts the sweetness, and pralines add crunch. Which whiskey the kitchen uses is a question for the chef, and ask the kitchen before saying whether the pralines are made in house.

Describe it warmly and plainly: soft, custardy bread pudding, whiskey caramel, tangy ice cream and pralines for crunch. Tell anyone who avoids alcohol that the caramel carries whiskey. Every question about eggs, nuts or anything else in the dish goes to the kitchen and the service note.

faults.fault: Wet and eggy in the middle
faults.cause: Underbaked, or too much custard for the bread.
faults.fix: Bake until a knife near the centre comes out clean and only the very middle wobbles.

faults.cause: Baked too long or too hot, so the eggs curdled.
faults.fix: Use a moderate oven and a water bath, and take it out as soon as the centre sets.

faults.cause: Too short a soak, or bread too dense.
faults.fix: Press the bread down and rest it 20 to 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.

faults.cause: The egg overheated and scrambled, and the butter separated.
faults.fix: Temper the egg with a little of the hot butter and sugar, whisk off the heat, or bind it with cream.

brennans.how: Warm bread pudding under a whiskey caramel, amber caramel loosened with cream and butter, with buttermilk ice cream for tang and pralines for crunch; the whiskey's name is a question for the chef.

cards.front: What is New Orleans bread pudding?
cards.back: Stale French bread soaked in a custard of milk or cream, eggs, sugar, vanilla and spice, often with raisins, baked until set and served warm with sauce.

cards.front: Why does New Orleans French bread make good bread pudding?
cards.back: Its light, airy crumb and thin crust stale fast and drink custard while keeping their shape; dense bread bakes heavy, fresh bread turns to paste.

cards.front: How much custard should the bread take?
cards.back: Enough to saturate it without leaving it swimming: every piece soaked through, with no deep pool of custard below.

cards.front: Why rest the soaked bread before baking?
cards.back: So the custard reaches the centre of every piece: 20 to 30 minutes, or covered overnight in the fridge, prevents dry cores.

cards.front: What is a sound starting ratio for bread pudding?
cards.back: About 450 g (1 lb) of stale French bread to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of milk or milk and cream, with 4 to 6 eggs and 150 to 250 g (5 to 9 oz) sugar.

cards.front: How do you know a bread pudding is done?
cards.back: Set at the centre: a knife near the middle comes out clean and only the very middle wobbles; a probe reads about 71 to 77°C (160 to 171°F).

cards.front: What happens when a bread pudding bakes too long or too hot?
cards.back: The custard curdles, weeping liquid and turning grainy and dry; a moderate oven and a water bath keep it smooth.

cards.front: What goes into a classic New Orleans whiskey sauce?
cards.back: Butter and sugar melted together, bound with a beaten egg or with cream, finished with bourbon and poured warm.

cards.front: Why does a whiskey sauce bound with egg split?
cards.back: Too much heat: the egg scrambles and the butter separates. Temper the egg with a little hot butter and sugar, and whisk off the heat.

cards.front: How long has bread pudding been in New Orleans cookbooks?
cards.back: Since the nineteenth century; restaurants revived it from the 1970s with whiskey and bourbon sauces, now its signature.

cards.front: What comes on Brennan's New Orleans Bread Pudding?
cards.back: A whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream for tang and pralines for crunch; the caramel carries whiskey, so tell guests who avoid alcohol.

questions.q: Why does New Orleans French bread suit bread pudding?
distractors: Its dense crumb resists the custard
Its rich dough adds butter and sugar
It stays fresh for a week
questions.why: A light, airy, lean crumb stales fast and soaks up custard without collapsing; dense or rich bread bakes heavy.

questions.q: How should the bread look after soaking, just before it goes into the oven?
distractors: Dry on top, so it crisps
Floating in a deep pool of custard
Barely damp, to keep it light
questions.why: Every piece should be soaked through; too little custard leaves dry patches, too much leaves a wet, eggy pool under the bread.

questions.q: Why is the soaked bread rested before baking?
questions.answer: So the custard reaches every centre
distractors: So the eggs begin to set
So the raisins sink to the bottom
So the bread can go stale
questions.why: Stale bread drinks slowly; a rest of 20 to 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge, lets the custard soak right through.

questions.q: Which sign shows a bread pudding is done?
questions.answer: A knife near the centre comes out clean
distractors: The whole dish wobbles when nudged
The top is still pale and wet to the touch
questions.why: A set centre gives a clean knife and only a slight wobble at the very middle; a loose dish is underbaked.

questions.q: A bread pudding weeps liquid and tastes grainy. What went wrong?
questions.answer: It baked too long or too hot
distractors: The custard had too little sugar
questions.why: Overheated eggs curdle and squeeze out liquid; a moderate oven, a water bath and pulling it as the centre sets prevent it.

questions.q: What binds the butter and sugar in a classic New Orleans whiskey sauce?
distractors: A roux of flour and butter
questions.why: The melted butter and sugar are bound with a tempered egg or with cream, then finished with bourbon; a roux, a starch slurry or gelatine has no place in it.

questions.q: Why does a whiskey sauce bound with egg split?
distractors: The bourbon goes in too late
It was whisked off the heat
questions.why: Too much heat sets the egg and lets the butter separate; tempering the egg and whisking off the heat keeps the sauce smooth.

questions.q: Which three things come with Brennan's New Orleans Bread Pudding?
questions.answer: Whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines
distractors: Rum sauce, vanilla ice cream and pecans
Whiskey sauce, whipped cream and raisins
Caramel custard, nougat ice cream and peanuts
questions.why: The house pairs the warm pudding with a whiskey caramel, tangy buttermilk ice cream and pralines; the custard and nougat belong to The Snickers.
